title: Lecture #22: Most Important Class in Java

questions.question: Given `class Human { }` and `class Student extends Human { }`, which statement is correct?
options: `Student` still inherits `toString()`, `equals()` and `hashCode()` from `Object`, through `Human`
`Student` no longer inherits from `Object`, because it already extends `Human`
`Student` must write `extends Human, Object` to keep `Object`'s methods
Only classes with no `extends` clause get `Object`'s methods
questions.explanation: Every class in Java ultimately inherits from `java.lang.Object`. A class with no `extends` clause implicitly extends `Object`, so `Human` extends `Object` and `Student` reaches `Object` through `Human`. Java has single class inheritance, so `extends Human, Object` would not compile, and it is not needed.

questions.question: What does this program print (one value per line)?
options: `Animal`, `Animal`, `false`, `true`
`Animal`, `Dog`, `true`, `true`
`Animal`, `Dog`, `false`, `true`
`Animal`, `Animal`, `false`, `false`
questions.explanation: `getClass()` returns the runtime class of the object, not the declared type of the variable, so `d.getClass().getName()` is `Dog`. `instanceof` checks whether the object is an instance of the class or any subclass: a plain `Animal` is not a `Dog` (false), but a `Dog` is an `Animal` (true).

questions.question: Your log line `System.out.println("Saved: " + student);` prints something like `Saved: Student@1b6d3586` instead of the student's name and age. What is the right fix?
options: Call `student.hashCode()` instead, which returns the student's data as text
Cast the object: `(String) student`
Override `equals()` in `Student`, because printing uses `equals()` to find the fields
Override `public String toString()` in `Student` to return the fields you want
questions.explanation: String concatenation and `println` call the object's `toString()`. `Object`'s default version returns `ClassName@hexHashCode`, which is what you see. Overriding `toString()` (as the lecture's `Student` does with `name + " , " + age`) gives a readable representation; casting a `Student` to `String` does not compile.

questions.question: Using the lecture's `Student` class shown below, what does `main` print?
options: `false`, `true`, `true`, `Aditya , 28`
`true`, `true`, `true`, `Aditya , 28`
`false`, `true`, `false`, `Student@` followed by a hex code
`false`, `false`, `true`, `Aditya , 28`
questions.explanation: `s1 == s2` compares references, and these are two different objects, so it is false. The overridden `equals()` compares name and age, which match, so it is true, and `Objects.hash(name, age)` gives equal hash codes for equal fields. `println(s1)` uses the overridden `toString()`, giving `Aditya , 28`.

questions.question: Two `Student` objects return the same value from `hashCode()`. What can you conclude?
options: They are definitely equal according to `equals()`
They are the same object in memory
Nothing certain: equal objects must have equal hash codes, but unequal objects may also share a hash code
At least one of them has a broken `hashCode()` implementation
questions.explanation: The rule only works in one direction: if `a.equals(b)` is true, their hash codes must be equal. The reverse does not hold, as the notes show with "Aditya" and "Rohit" both drawn with hash 123; such collisions are legal. A shared hash code therefore says nothing definite about equality or identity.
questions.source: notes p3 (rule: if two objects are equal their hashCode must be equal, reverse may not be true)

questions.question: A teammate overrides `equals()` in `Student` to compare name and age but does not override `hashCode()`. They add `s1` to a `HashSet`, then call `set.contains(s2)` where `s2` has the same name and age; it returns `false`. Why?
options: `HashSet` never calls `equals()`; it only compares references with `==`
The set first uses `hashCode()` to locate the bucket; `Object`'s default hash codes for the two distinct objects differ, so `equals()` is never even tried on `s1`
`contains()` requires `Student` to implement `Comparable`
Overriding `equals()` automatically disables the default `hashCode()`, so the set throws away the lookup
questions.explanation: Hash-based collections (`HashSet`, `HashMap`, `Hashtable`) use `hashCode()` to pick a bucket and only then call `equals()` on entries in that bucket. With the default `Object.hashCode()`, two distinct objects practically always get different values, so the lookup goes to the wrong bucket. That is why the equal-objects-equal-hash-codes rule exists and both methods must be overridden together.
questions.source: notes p3 (HashSet, HashMap, Hashtable); code: Demo.java

questions.question: A class overrides `clone()` with `return super.clone();` but does NOT implement `Cloneable`. What happens when `clone()` is called on one of its objects?
options: It returns a deep copy, because `Cloneable` is only needed for shallow copies
It fails to compile, because `Cloneable` declares the `clone()` method that must be implemented
It returns `null`, since the class did not opt in to cloning
`Object.clone()` throws `CloneNotSupportedException` at runtime
questions.explanation: `Cloneable` is a marker interface: it is empty, and `Object.clone()` merely checks whether the object's class implements it. If not, it throws `CloneNotSupportedException`; if so, it returns a field-by-field (shallow) copy. Because the interface declares no methods, leaving it out is not a compile error.
questions.source: notes p4 (Cloneable as marker interface); code: Demo.java

questions.question: The lecture's `equals()` compares names with `==`. What does this program print?
options: `true` then `true`
`false` then `true`
`false` then `false`
`true` then `false`
questions.explanation: `first + "tya"` is computed at runtime (since `first` is not a constant), producing a new `String` object that is not the pooled literal `"Aditya"`. So `this.name == s.name` is false and `equals()` returns false, even though the texts match. `Objects.hash` uses `String.hashCode()`, which depends only on the characters, so the hash codes are equal; the fix is to compare with `Objects.equals(name, s.name)`.

questions.question: `Student implements Cloneable` and has an `int[] marks` field; its `clone()` just returns `super.clone()`. After `Student s3 = (Student) s1.clone(); s3.marks[0] = 50;`, `s1.marks[0]` is also 50. What explains this, and what is the fix?
options: `clone()` returned the same object, so `s3 == s1`; implement `Cloneable` correctly to get a new object
Arrays are primitives, so they are shared automatically; declare `marks` as `final` to stop sharing
`Object.clone()` makes a shallow copy, so both objects reference the same array; override `clone()` to also copy the array (e.g. `copy.marks = marks.clone()`)
The JVM caches cloned arrays; call `System.gc()` before cloning
questions.explanation: `Object.clone()` creates a new `Student` (`s3 != s1`), but copies each field as if by assignment, so the reference `marks` points to the same array in both objects: a shallow copy. A deep copy requires overriding `clone()` to copy the mutable parts too. Arrays are objects, not primitives, and `final` only stops reassigning the field.
questions.source: notes p4 (clone: shallow copy; override for deep copy; arrays are objects)

questions.question: The lecture's `equals()` rejects the argument when `obj.getClass() != this.getClass()`. Suppose `class Monitor extends Student` and a `Monitor` and a `Student` have the same name and age. What does this check imply?
options: They compare equal, because a `Monitor` is an instance of `Student`
They are never equal, because their runtime classes differ; this also keeps `equals()` symmetric between parent and child
`equals()` throws `ClassCastException` because the cast `(Student) obj` runs first
They compare equal only if `Monitor` also overrides `hashCode()`
questions.explanation: `getClass()` returns the exact runtime class, so a `Monitor` and a `Student` are rejected before any field comparison, keeping the result the same whichever object you call it on. An `instanceof Student` check would accept a `Monitor` and could make `student.equals(monitor)` differ from `monitor.equals(student)` if `Monitor` overrides `equals()`. The class check runs before the cast, which is exactly what prevents a `ClassCastException`.
questions.source: code: Demo.java (equals with getClass check); code: Demo2.java
